words.definition: a particular way of viewing and interpreting an environmental issue
words.example: Different communities may interpret the same conservation policy from different perspectives.

words.definition: beliefs about what is important, desirable or morally right
words.example: Values influence how people judge the importance of economic growth and habitat protection.

words.definition: a broad set of beliefs through which a person understands society and nature
words.example: A person's worldview can shape their response to climate policy.

words.definition: a framework of beliefs used to evaluate environmental issues and choices
words.example: An environmental value system influences preferences for technology, conservation or reduced consumption.

words.definition: placing ecosystems and the intrinsic value of nature at the centre of decision-making
words.example: An ecocentric policy may protect a forest even when no direct economic benefit is expected.

words.definition: judging environmental issues mainly in terms of human needs and welfare
words.example: An anthropocentric argument may support conservation because healthy ecosystems benefit people.

words.definition: emphasizing technology and human innovation as solutions to environmental problems
words.example: A technocentric approach may favour carbon capture over reducing consumption.

words.definition: organized social action aimed at protecting the environment or changing environmental policy
words.example: The environmental movement helped place pollution control on the political agenda.

words.definition: a dominant pattern of ideas and assumptions that shapes how problems are understood
words.example: A shift in paradigm can change whether nature is viewed as a resource or as a system with intrinsic value.

words.definition: a person or group affected by or able to influence a decision
words.example: Farmers, residents and conservation groups are all stakeholders in river management.

words.definition: the effect of shared traditions, norms and practices on beliefs and behaviour
words.example: Cultural influence can affect attitudes toward wildlife, food and resource use.

words.definition: a set of ideas about how society and government should be organized
words.example: Political ideology may influence support for regulation or market-based environmental policies.

words.definition: the effect of religious beliefs and teachings on attitudes and actions
words.example: Religious influence can encourage stewardship or particular views about humanity's relationship with nature.

words.definition: the effect of news, advertising and digital communication on public understanding and behaviour
words.example: Media influence can increase concern about a disaster or spread misleading environmental claims.

words.definition: the process of developing knowledge, understanding and skills through learning
words.example: Environmental education can improve understanding of waste reduction and biodiversity.

words.definition: a person's or group's social and economic position based on factors such as income and education
words.example: Socio-economic status can affect exposure to pollution and access to environmental resources.

words.definition: a belief in and commitment to protecting natural systems from harmful human impacts
words.example: Environmentalism has influenced laws on endangered species and pollution.

words.definition: a tendency to expect favourable outcomes or believe problems can be solved
words.example: Technological optimism can increase confidence that innovation will reduce emissions.

words.definition: a tendency to expect unfavourable outcomes or doubt that problems will be solved
words.example: Environmental pessimism may arise when ecosystem decline continues despite policy action.

words.definition: a disagreement caused by different beliefs about what is important or morally acceptable
words.example: A value conflict may occur when local jobs depend on mining in a protected landscape.

words.definition: a set of interacting components that together form a functioning whole
words.example: A lake can be studied as a system with inputs, storages, transfers and outputs.

words.definition: an approach that focuses on relationships, feedbacks and interactions among components
words.example: Systems thinking helps explain why changing one part of a food web can affect many others.

words.definition: the defined limit separating the parts being studied from the surrounding environment
words.example: A watershed boundary can be used to define the system being investigated.

words.definition: matter, energy or information entering a system
words.example: Rainfall is an input to a drainage basin.

words.definition: matter, energy or information leaving a system
words.example: River discharge is an output from a drainage basin.

words.definition: movement of matter or energy from one storage to another without changing its form
words.japanese: 移動・トランスファー
words.example: Water moving from soil into a river is a transfer within the hydrological system.

words.definition: movement of matter, energy or information through a system
words.example: Energy flows through an ecosystem from producers to consumers.

words.definition: a place or component in which matter or energy is held for a period of time
words.example: A forest is an important carbon storage.

words.definition: a system that exchanges both matter and energy with its surroundings
words.example: Most ecosystems are open systems because organisms, nutrients and energy cross their boundaries.

words.definition: a system that exchanges energy but little or no matter with its surroundings
words.example: Earth is often approximated as a closed system for matter.

words.definition: a theoretical system that exchanges neither matter nor energy with its surroundings
words.example: A perfectly isolated system does not exist naturally on Earth.

words.definition: a process in which a change in a system influences the conditions that caused that change
words.example: Melting ice can trigger feedback by reducing surface reflectivity.

words.definition: a process that amplifies an initial change and pushes a system further from its starting state
words.example: Permafrost thaw can create positive feedback when released methane causes additional warming.

words.definition: a process that counteracts an initial change and tends to stabilize a system
words.example: Higher plant growth can create negative feedback by removing more carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

words.definition: a condition in which opposing processes are balanced overall
words.example: A population may fluctuate around equilibrium when births and deaths are approximately balanced.

words.definition: a dynamic condition in which inputs and outputs remain balanced over time despite internal change
words.example: A mature ecosystem may maintain steady-state equilibrium while individual organisms continue to change.

words.definition: a threshold beyond which a small additional change can cause a large and often difficult-to-reverse shift
words.japanese: 転換点・ティッピングポイント
words.example: Loss of enough ice cover could push a climate system beyond a tipping point.

words.definition: the ability of a system to remain largely unchanged when exposed to disturbance
words.example: A diverse grassland may show high resistance to a short drought.

words.definition: a characteristic of a whole system that arises from interactions among its parts
words.example: Ecosystem stability can be an emergent property of many interacting species.

words.definition: a simplified representation used to describe, explain or predict a system
words.example: Climate models simulate interactions among the atmosphere, oceans and land.

words.definition: the capacity to meet present needs while maintaining ecological, social and economic systems over the long term
words.example: Sustainability requires resource use that does not undermine future generations.

words.definition: development that improves human well-being without preventing future generations from meeting their needs
words.example: Renewable energy and efficient public transport can support sustainable development.

words.definition: the biologically productive area needed to supply a population's resources and absorb its wastes
words.japanese: エコロジカル・フットプリント
words.example: A diet high in resource-intensive foods can increase an individual's ecological footprint.

words.definition: the ability of biologically productive land and water to regenerate resources and absorb wastes
words.example: A country with extensive productive forests may have relatively high biocapacity.

words.definition: proposed limits for key Earth-system processes within which humanity can operate more safely
words.japanese: プラネタリー・バウンダリー
words.example: Climate change and biodiversity loss are included among the planetary boundaries.

words.definition: a condition in which human demand on ecosystems exceeds their regenerative capacity
words.example: Persistent ecological overshoot depletes natural capital.

words.definition: the amount by which a population's ecological footprint exceeds available biocapacity
words.example: A country may run an ecological deficit by consuming more resources than its ecosystems regenerate.

words.definition: the amount by which available biocapacity exceeds a population's ecological footprint
words.example: Low consumption and abundant productive land can produce an ecological surplus.

words.definition: fairness in the distribution of environmental benefits and costs between present and future generations
words.example: Protecting groundwater reserves supports intergenerational equity.

words.definition: fairness in the distribution of resources, risks and opportunities among people living at the same time
words.example: Equal access to clean water is an issue of intragenerational equity.

words.definition: use of goods and services in ways that reduce resource depletion and environmental harm
words.example: Repairing products and reducing waste are forms of sustainable consumption.

words.definition: creation of goods and services using methods that minimize resource use, pollution and ecosystem damage
words.example: Factories can support sustainable production by improving efficiency and recycling materials.

words.definition: obtaining more useful output from each unit of material, energy or water used
words.example: LED lighting improves resource efficiency by providing the same light with less electricity.

words.definition: a measurable variable used to assess environmental condition, pressure or progress
words.example: Dissolved oxygen can serve as an environmental indicator of river quality.

words.definition: planned actions used to monitor, regulate and reduce impacts on environmental systems
words.example: Wetland restoration can be part of environmental management in a river basin.

words.definition: the ability of an environment to absorb and process waste without unacceptable damage
words.example: A river's assimilation capacity can be exceeded when sewage inputs become too high.

words.definition: decline in environmental quality caused by resource depletion, pollution or ecosystem damage
words.example: Deforestation and soil erosion can cause long-term environmental degradation.

words.definition: an approach that evaluates performance in environmental, social and economic terms
words.japanese: トリプル・ボトムライン
words.example: A business using the triple bottom line considers profit, people and environmental impact.

words.definition: a long-term shift from unsustainable systems toward practices and technologies that can be maintained
words.example: Moving from fossil fuels to low-carbon energy is a sustainability transition.

words.definition: a pattern of living designed to reduce environmental impact while supporting well-being
words.example: Using public transport and consuming fewer disposable products can support a sustainable lifestyle.
